Project 01 · Digital banking

Redesigning Pay & Transfer for faster, clearer everyday payments.

I redesigned AIB’s Pay & Transfer journey across payee setup, IBAN validation, instant payments, authentication and daily-limit recovery. The work focused on making common transfers easier to complete while keeping security and payment status clear.

RoleSenior Product Designer
ScopeDiscovery, product strategy, interaction, UI, prototyping, design system
PlatformiOS & Android
DomainPayments, risk, authentication

AIB MOBILE BANKING

A banking experience designed around clarity, speed and trust.

Context

Pay & Transfer needed to become easier without weakening the controls around a bank transfer.

More banking activity was moving to mobile and online channels in Ireland, while payment fraud kept security central to the experience. For Pay & Transfer, that meant reducing unnecessary steps in routine transfers without treating higher-risk actions the same way.

Evidence before solutions

I used the benchmark to compare specific interaction patterns, not to copy complete flows.

I reviewed Revolut, N26 and Monzo for patterns already common in digital banking, and Pix as a reference from a different payment context. I compared real-time validation, contact payments, transaction feedback and limit handling, then decided what made sense for AIB.

01
Validation before commitment

Customers should know whether an IBAN is valid before submitting the form.

02
Identity before account detail

When possible, choosing a person should feel closer to messaging than filling a bank form.

03
Guardrails need exits

A security limit can protect customers without forcing a support call.

Design principle

The audit surfaced four interaction problems I could address.

IBAN errors appeared too late, Pay a Contact sat outside the main transfer path, completed steps gave little feedback, and the daily limit could stop a transfer without a clear recovery path. These became the four areas I focused on.

payment flow

I mapped what had to happen before, during and after a transfer.

Instead of treating each screen separately, I mapped the information and checks needed across the full transfer.

Daily limit strategy

The €10k daily limit needed a recovery path inside the transfer.

The existing limit could block a legitimate high-value transfer. I explored how to let the customer continue without making the higher limit permanent.

Scenario
Customer needs to send €14,000 · Daily limit €10,000
OPTION A

Block

Stop the transfer and direct the customer to support.

Low exposure · Low autonomy
OPTION B

Permanent increase

Raise the ceiling and keep it higher for future transfers.

High autonomy · Higher lasting exposure
DECISION · C

Temporary elevation

Strong authentication, time-bounded increase and automatic reset.

Autonomy with temporary exposure
CUSTOMER
Complete now

No support call for a legitimate high-value transfer.

RISK
Bound exposure

The higher ceiling exists only for a defined window.

SECURITY
Verify intent

Strong authentication protects the change in risk.

SYSTEM
Reset automatically

The safer default returns without another customer action.

€14k requested→Limit detected→Temporary increase→Face ID→Continue transfer→Auto reset

Risk × friction

I added stronger authentication only when the level of risk changed.

Routine transfers kept the standard confirmation path. A temporary limit increase required stronger authentication because it changed the customer’s exposure.

ActionRiskProduct response
Choose saved payeeLOWNo additional friction
Add a new IBANMEDIUMReal-time account validation
Send standard transferMEDIUMReview and standard confirmation
Increase daily limitHIGHStrong authentication + time-bound change
High-value transferHIGHExplicit review + elevated assurance
Security should not add friction everywhere. It should appear where risk changes.

Designing trust

I checked what the customer needed to know at each point in the transfer.

Before submission, the customer needs to confirm the recipient and amount. During processing, the product needs to show that the instruction is being handled. Afterward, the outcome and receipt need to be unambiguous.

BEFORE

Am I sending the right money to the right person?

Recipient identity · IBAN · receiving bank · amount · payment method

DURING

Is the bank actually processing my instruction?

Authentication · locked CTA · processing state · duplicate prevention

AFTER

Did the money move, and can I prove it?

Outcome · timestamp · reference · receipt · recovery when uncertain

TRUST BUILDS THROUGHIdentity→Validation→Review→Authentication→Status→Receipt

Decision 01

Decision 01

Move IBAN validation into the form.

Problem

The existing form could leave an IBAN problem until submission.

Decision

I moved validation into the form, showed the receiving bank when available and gave the customer a specific correction when the IBAN could not be accepted.

Trade-off

This adds feedback while the customer is typing, but reduces uncertainty before the transfer is submitted.

Decision 02

Decision 02

Bring Pay a Contact into the main recipient flow.

Problem

Pay a Contact existed, but it was separated from the main transfer entry point and required customers to find it first.

Decision

I brought Contact alongside the other recipient options so the journey could start with who the customer wanted to pay.

Trade-off

A contact-first entry point means someone paying a first-time payee without a phone-linked account still needs the manual or IBAN path. It cannot fully disappear.

Decision 03

Decision 03

Add explicit feedback after actions that affect the transfer.

I added feedback where customers needed confirmation that an action had been accepted, was still processing or had completed.

Problem

Several steps previously changed with little confirmation that the action had been accepted.

Decision

The redesign uses contextual feedback, including SEPA Instant availability while entering the amount and a receipt after completion.

Trade-off

More design surface to build and maintain than a single generic loading state.

Interaction detail

Recovery flow

Let customers recover from the daily limit without leaving the transfer.

Problem

A permanent limit increase would create more exposure than the immediate transfer required. A hard stop, however, could push a legitimate customer to support.

Decision

I designed a temporary increase that asks for the new amount, requires Face ID and returns to the previous limit automatically after 24 hours.

Trade-off

A temporary increase that reverts automatically could surprise someone who expected it to stay. The copy has to carry that weight.

Trade-offs

The main trade-offs came from speed, security and recoverability.

Speed × Security
Flexibility × Fraud exposure
Automation × Customer control
Minimal UI × Explicit feedback

I kept routine actions light and added extra steps when the customer changed the level of risk, such as temporarily increasing the daily limit.

Cross-functional decisions

Some decisions required alignment with Product, Security and Engineering because the UI depended on what the system could verify and when.

DESIGN × ENGINEERING

IBAN validation

Question
When can the product confidently identify an account?

Constraint
Validation may be asynchronous or temporarily unavailable.

Outcome
Checking, valid, invalid and unable-to-verify became explicit current states.

DESIGN × PRODUCT × RISK

Daily limit

Question
How do we unblock legitimate high-value transfers?

Constraint
A permanent increase expands exposure beyond the immediate need.

Outcome
Temporary elevation, strong authentication and automatic reset.

DESIGN × SECURITY × ENGINEERING

Authentication

Question
Where should stronger authentication appear?

Constraint
Repeated security prompts make routine payments unnecessarily heavy.

Outcome
Authentication appears when risk changes, while transaction context is preserved.

Those discussions changed the states, authentication points and recovery behaviour in the final flow.

Final experience

The final flow covered five stages across thirteen screens.

The screens follow the order of the customer task: choose a recipient, validate details, enter the amount, confirm security checks and see the outcome.

01ChooseSaved · Contact · New
02IdentifyIBAN · Bank · Eligibility
03TransferAmount · Rail · Review
04SecureRisk · Limit · Face ID
05ResolveProcessing · Receipt · Recovery
Design intent

Each screen focuses on the decision available at that step and keeps enough context for the customer to understand what happens next.

Components & states

Components were defined around the states used in the transfer.

I tied component variants to concrete states such as checking, valid, invalid, unavailable, processing and completed. This gave Engineering a clearer set of behaviours to implement.

IBAN FIELD

Account validation

default → focus → checking → valid → invalid → unavailable

UI mirrors whether the account is unknown, being checked, identified or unresolved.

PAYEE

Recipient identity

saved → contact → new → selected → unavailable

Different entry paths resolve into one recipient model.

payment method

Transfer eligibility

SEPA → instant available → selected → unavailable

Availability is a product condition, not a decorative toggle.

AMOUNT

Risk boundary

default → filled → approaching limit → over limit

The amount component becomes a risk surface when thresholds change.

AUTHENTICATION

Intent verification

idle → required → authenticating → verified → failed

Security state stays connected to the transaction being approved.

PRIMARY CTA

Submission control

default → disabled → loading → locked → complete

CTA behaviour prevents accidental resubmission while state is unresolved.

FEEDBACK

System communication

info → success → warning → recoverable error

Feedback communicates consequence and next action, not just severity.

TRANSACTION

Money movement

draft → processing → completed → failed → unknown

Transaction status is treated separately from interface/network status.

SYSTEM PRINCIPLE

The component reflects the state of the product. Variants exist because behaviour changes, not because a Figma file needs more options.

Edge-case system

I designed recovery states alongside the main transfer flow.

ScenarioPreventCommunicateRecover
Invalid IBANValidate before commitmentExplain what is wrongEdit inline, preserve value
Instant unavailableCheck rail eligibilityExplain timing changeContinue with SEPA
Limit exceededCheck before submissionShow available limitTemporary elevation
Authentication failedKeep transaction contextExplain verification failureRetry authentication safely
Transfer processingLock duplicate submissionShow explicit statusWait for known state
Connection lostPreserve transaction intentAcknowledge uncertaintyCheck transaction status before retry

Where recovery was possible, the flow preserved recipient, amount and transaction context instead of making the customer start again.

Transaction certainty

An interrupted transfer needed a clear status before the customer could try again.

If the connection drops after confirmation, the customer may not know whether the transfer was submitted. I treated that separately from a normal failure and blocked another submission until the transaction status was known.

01Confirm

Customer commits.

02Lock

CTA cannot submit twice.

03Process

Transaction is pending.

04Resolve

Check confirmed transaction status.

05Recover

Retry only when safe.

STATE LOGIC
review
↓
authenticating
↓
processing ──→ completed → receipt
│
├──→ failed → safe retry
└──→ unknown → status check → resolve

Accessibility

Accessibility checks focused on information that affects the transfer.

Important information could not depend only on colour, animation or precise interaction. Labels, status text, focus order and touch targets were reviewed alongside the visual states.

€5,000.00Amount

Hierarchy, label and formatting communicate the value. Size or colour never carries meaning alone.

!Invalid IBAN

Error uses icon, text and actionable guidance, not red alone.

✓Transfer completed

Success is explicit in copy and announced as a state change, rather than depending on green feedback.

•••Processing

Loading has a textual status, prevents duplicate action and does not rely on animation to explain what is happening.

Face IDAuthentication failure

Failure preserves context and provides a clear recovery route instead of restarting the payment.

44px+Interaction

Primary actions use comfortable touch targets, visible focus and predictable order across the journey.

Prototype & handoff

The handoff included behaviour and states, not only final screens.

Prototype

Default, focus, valid, invalid, loading and disabled. Shared interaction logic reduces one-off implementation.

04
QA

Visual and interaction review against designed states. Edge cases checked with the same rigor as the happy path.

Engineering handoff

I documented what should happen between the screens.

The handoff covered when validation starts, what remains after a recoverable error, when the primary action locks and how an uncertain transaction is resolved.

Behaviour specification
01Validate IBAN asynchronously and expose Checking before a result is known.
02Preserve recipient, amount and payment context after recoverable errors.
03Lock the primary action while a transfer is processing to prevent duplicate intent.
04Do not offer Retry until the previous transaction state is known.
05Return from authentication to the same transaction context.
06Expire the temporary limit automatically after the defined window.
Transaction state
review
↓

↓
processing
├─ completed → receipt
├─ failed → recovery
└─ unknown → status check

Design QA checks the implementation against state logic, not only visual parity.

Measurement framework

I defined the measures I would use to evaluate the redesigned journey after launch.

The measurement plan focused on transfer completion, time to complete, validation errors, duplicate attempts, self-service limit recovery and post-transfer confidence. These are evaluation criteria for this redesign, not reported results.

NORTH STAR
Successful self-service transfers
01CompletionTransfer completion rate
02SpeedMedian time to complete
03QualityIBAN errors · duplicate attempts
04RecoverySelf-service limit recovery
05ConfidencePost-transfer confidence / CSAT
What I would watch

I would read completion time together with validation errors, duplicate attempts, support contacts and recovery rate. A shorter flow would not be an improvement if it created more uncertainty or failed transfers.

How the evidence in this case is presented.

R

Some diagrams and component labels were reorganized for this case so the work is easier to review. They do not represent AIB’s internal naming conventions.

Reflection

The main lesson was to make status and recovery as clear as the happy path.

This project changed how I approach financial flows. I now map validation, failure and recovery earlier, because those states affect the main interaction as much as the happy path does.
